papers.title: The Role of Parental Beliefs and Public Policies in Financing Higher Education: An Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded. This study examines how parental beliefs and future borrowing costs shape college saving decisions. Through a survey experiment with an embedded financial planning tool, we elicit parental beliefs about the future costs of college and their expectations of different funding sources, including financial aid and student loans. We find that nearly all parents want to cover some of the future costs of college, but many may fall short in their savings due to underestimating future expenses and overestimating available financial aid. A corrective information intervention encourages most parents to recalibrate their saving target. However, when a substantial gap between expected and actual costs is combined with a salient high repayment burden for their child, we find a discouragement effect that diminishes both their willingness to save and their aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. We calibrate a model of parental saving with learning about college costs, which reproduces both the absence of an average response to borrowing costs and the shift of children away from college attendance, and use it to price the welfare cost of misperception. Parents with higher financial literacy hold better-calibrated beliefs and respond more to correction. We discuss policy implications for outreach activities to support informed financial planning for college education.

papers.title: Aging and Structural Change: Cost Disease in the Care Sector
papers.abstract: For most of the service sector, market productivity growth has pulled production out of the home. We show that formal nursing care is an exception because its productivity growth has been negative. A two-sector general equilibrium overlapping generations model with informal care attributes the rise in formal care's relative price to this decline, not demography. Care/non-care complementarity dominates formal/informal complementarity. As formal prices rise, elders substitute non-care consumption for formal care, shifting care onto informal caregivers. Population aging need not slow growth if non-care productivity rises or entering cohorts grow and its effects are offset by declining care needs.

papers.title: The Health Effects of Eating Red Meat: A Natural Experiment in Alpha-Gal Syndrome
papers.abstract: Observational associations between red meat consumption and cardiometabolic disease are confounded by diet and other health behaviors. Alpha-gal syndrome, a tick-borne allergy to mammalian meat, leads to an abrupt and involuntary cessation of red meat consumption. Using national electronic health records, we compared changes in weight and cardiometabolic health over two years before and after newly detected alpha-gal syndrome with those in patients with other tick-borne diseases, who were also bitten and sought care but whose diagnoses carry no dietary restriction. Relative to this comparison group, diagnosis of alpha-gal syndrome led to a sustained 0.8 kg (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.0) reduction in body weight that increased with the degree of sensitization, as well as small reductions in triglycerides, glycated hemoglobin, glucose, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Not eating red meat appears to yield modest but measurable cardiometabolic benefits.

papers.title: Crash Injuries and Fatalities in the United States Following Standardization of Automatic Emergency Braking
papers.abstract: Whether vehicle safety technologies reduce crash injuries and fatalities is relevant to consumers and regulators, but rigorous real world evidence is limited because drivers who choose optional features differ from those who do not. As a natural experiment, we leveraged the staggered implementation of automatic emergency braking as standard rather than optional equipment on 39 vehicle models between 2017 and 2022. Across the United States, the percentage of crash injuries from rear-end collisions caused by the vehicle fell from 13.9% to 8.0% at the first standard model year, and the percentage of crash fatalities fell from 6.0% to 4.7%. Neither fell in models that never standardized the technology, and crash types it was not designed to prevent were unaffected. Automatic emergency braking reduces crash injuries and fatalities.

papers.title: Childhood Learning and Adult Earnings in Four LMIC Cohorts
papers.abstract: Researchers and policymakers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have customarily relied on indirect evidence to justify investments in learning, either by linking test scores to economic growth or by connecting adult cognitive assessments to earnings. This reliance on indirect evidence largely stems from the scarcity of longitudinal data linking school-age learning to adult earnings. We address this gap by using data from Ethiopia, India, Pakistan, and Peru to estimate associations between foundational learning (FL), measured by test scores around age 12, and human capital and earnings in young adulthood. In Peru, India, and Pakistan, a one-standard-deviation increase in FL is associated with an 8-13 log point increase in adult earnings. Childhood scores also predict 1.1-1.5 additional years of schooling and 9.3-13.5 percentage points higher college or vocational attendance, as well as higher skills in adulthood. Interestingly, a linear-projection decomposition indicates that measured schooling and adult test scores explain between 18% (Peru) to 50-56% (India and Pakistan) of the FL-earnings gradient, suggesting that FL may raise earnings over and above the association with schooling and adult scores. Finally, FL can account for about 5-12 percent of the earnings gap between young Ethiopians and Indians in our sample, a number that could rise to 33 percent as returns to learning grow over the life cycle. We interpret these descriptive findings in light of recent causal evidence on the learning-to-earnings pipeline and discuss the implications for policy investments in FL.

papers.title: Learn to Earn: The Long-Term Effects of Foundational Learning
papers.abstract: Tracking Pakistani students over 15 years, we use two identification strategies to provide the first causal evidence linking learning in primary school to adult outcomes in a low-income country. Exposure to a school with higher test score value-added increases educational attainment and earnings 15 years later. A randomized information intervention that led to learning gains at the village level generated similar effects. Lifetime earnings gains across all students attending a 1sd better school total US$175,000, and for the information intervention, the marginal value of public funds is infinity for men. There is a strong economic case for investing in learning.

papers.title: A Blessing in Disguise: The Long-Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old-Age Male Longevity
papers.abstract: The infamous agricultural pest, the boll weevil, spread across southern US counties between 1892 and 1920. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. We show that the estimated effects are robust across a wide array of specifications, are not driven by sociodemographic and socioeconomic compositional change in the final sample, and are not associated with pre-existing trends in the outcome. Further, we find larger impacts among Blacks, children of lower educated mothers, whose fathers work in the farming industry, and those born in high cotton intensity counties. Moreover, the effects appear to be substantially larger among children in states with less restrictive child labor policies, implying the role of these policies in reducing the adverse effects of child labor in the absence of the boll weevil in cotton production counties. Affected children are more likely to migrate, and their destination counties are more likely to be urban and have higher socioeconomic scores. The 1940 census suggests that the exposed children attain higher levels of education and have higher socioeconomic scores. We discuss the policy implications of these results in relation to child labor and school attendance policies in developing countries.

papers.title: Preconception Medicaid and Maternal and Infant Health: Evidence from Linked Administrative Data
papers.abstract: Despite pregnancy-focused public insurance coverage in the U.S., low-income mothers and infants face persistent health disadvantages. Using linked birth, tax, and enrollment data, we examine the effects of preconception coverage from California's 2014 Medicaid expansion, comparing changes in outcomes for first-time mothers just below and above the income eligibility threshold. Expansion increased preconception Medicaid enrollment by 3.4 months (+23 percentage points in 12-month continuous coverage), first-month pregnancy enrollment by 24 percentage points, and adequate prenatal care and STI screening. Yet we find no improvements in maternal or infant health, suggesting preconception coverage alone cannot close health disparities.

papers.title: How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances?
papers.abstract: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

papers.title: Education and Gender Voting Polarization: The Effect of Compulsory Schooling on Sex-Based Preferences for the Democratic and Republican Parties
papers.abstract: One of the most notable developments in U.S. electoral politics over the last 40 years is the increasing divide between men and women voters. While men and women had roughly equivalent levels of support for both the Democratic and Republican parties in 1980, more recent surveys have revealed a roughly 10 to 15-percentage-point gap in preference for the Democratic party among women relative to men. We explain this result by using a variety of econometric strategies to establish a novel connection between compulsory schooling laws (CSLs), educational attainment, and diverging political preferences by sex. First, we show that the timing of this divergence is coincident with recent changes in CSLs, and that this divergence is almost entirely due to changes in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party in states where there exists a much stronger effect of CSLs on average educational attainment -- very little change in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party is present in other states. Furthermore, in states with more-impactful CSLs, changes in CSLs and their associated increased educational attainment explain almost all of the diverging support for political parties and differences in opinion over major policy issues by sex, such as gun control and abortion. Altogether, these new facts present an original explanation that relies upon the effect of education to explain the evolution of gender political preferences in the U.S. over the last 40 years.

papers.title: Decoding Success: Phonics-based Instruction and Student Achievement
papers.abstract: Reading is a foundational skill, yet fewer than one in three US fourth graders read at a proficient level. How best to teach reading and improve educational attainment has been an active policy debate for decades. Recently, phonics-based approaches have surged in popularity, even though the largest attempt to put similar methods into classrooms was previously abandoned out of concerns that the program was ineffective. This paper studies Reading First, a nearly $1 billion per year federal program established under No Child Left Behind that promoted phonics-based instruction in K-3 classrooms. Exploiting administrative data from Texas and program eligibility formulas, we estimate effects via difference-in-differences and instrumental variables specifications. We find that eligibility increased third-grade reading test scores by 0.1 standard deviations and that effects persisted through at least the eighth grade. An analysis of digitized exam questions shows that treated students outperformed peers on questions that required basic decoding skills and those with more words, a benefit that also drove improvements in math scores. We follow exposed cohorts into early adulthood, finding that the program increased on-time high school graduation, college enrollment, four-year college completion, and adult earnings at age 25.

papers.title: Economics of Mental Health
papers.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of the rapidly evolving economics literature on mental health, focusing on research published since 2015. This literature has grown substantially, reflecting the increased recognition of the prevalence and economic costs of mental illness, declining stigma, and the growing availability of data on mental health. In addition to the economic costs of mental illness, the review focuses on four broad classes of determinants of mental health: endowments, economic resources, education, and trauma. We also examine the determinants and effects of mental health treatment. Finally, we discuss how certain features of mental illness, including its episodic and recurrent nature, pose challenges for the canonical health capital model.

papers.title: The Effects of Years of Health Insurance on the Health of Older Adults
papers.abstract: Whether longer exposure to health insurance improves health remains an open empirical question. This study examines the health effects of an additional year of health insurance coverage by exploiting differential changes in coverage pre-to-post implementation of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) for those who were and were not insured prior to the ACA. Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), we instrument for insurance duration using baseline uninsured status interacted with the post-ACA period. We find that the ACA increased insurance coverage by approximately one additional year among previously uninsured respondents relative to those insured at baseline. Instrumental-variable estimates provide no statistically significant evidence of improvements in self-rated health, depressive symptoms, or hypertension over a four-year follow-up period. These findings are robust across alternative specifications. Overall, results provide little evidence that longer insurance coverage translates into measurable short-term health improvements, while leaving open the possibility of modest or longer-term benefits.

papers.title: Impacts of AI in Higher Education: A Panel Survey of Undergraduates
papers.abstract: We report findings from the first wave of a survey of undergraduates including separate samples of Dartmouth students, graduating high school seniors, and U.S. college students more broadly. Students report extensive use of AI both for tasks which are likely harmful to learning and tasks which are likely helpful to learning. Students report much higher peer misuse of AI relative to reports of own misuse. Ninety-two percent of students agree or strongly agree that use of AI is harmful to writing. Use of graded out-of-class assignments has become increasingly unfair due to cheating with AI. But students see the value of using AI to answer conceptual questions in real time, create practice quizzes and study guides and to enable meaningful and efficient progress on research projects. Eighty-four percent of Dartmouth respondents report that AI is changing the nature of jobs in their desired (future) field as opposed to eliminating jobs. AI’s perceived value and harms vary widely by academic discipline suggesting that use, rules, and approaches must also vary greatly based on the discipline and context. Students are largely self-taught in AI but have strong demand for incorporating AI effectively in the curriculum.
